subject: Cloud Computing
title: Retry with Exponential Backoff
description: A 60-second lesson on Retry with Exponential Backoff.

hook.text: A request fails. You retry immediately. It fails again. You retry faster. Now you're DDoS-ing your own system.

buildup.text: Exponential backoff spaces retries further apart: 1 second, 2 seconds, 4 seconds, 8 seconds, and so on.

discovery.text: Adding random jitter prevents all clients from retrying at the exact same moment — a thundering herd.

twist.text: Without backoff, a temporary glitch becomes a permanent outage. Retries pile up faster than the server can recover.

climax.text: Every cloud SDK uses exponential backoff by default. It's the simplest resilience pattern and one of the most important.

punchline.text: Retry gently. Give the system time to breathe and recover.

quiz.question: Why is random jitter added to exponential backoff?
options: To prevent all clients from retrying at the same time and overwhelming the server
To make requests arrive in alphabetical order
To encrypt retry attempts for security

details.summary: Exponential backoff retries failed requests with increasing delays between attempts. Adding random jitter prevents many clients from retrying simultaneously. This pattern handles transient failures gracefully without overwhelming the recovering service.
details.whyItMatters: Transient failures are inevitable in distributed systems. Smart retry logic prevents thundering herds that can turn a minor hiccup into a major outage.
takeaways: Delays increase exponentially with each retry attempt
Random jitter prevents synchronized retry storms
Handles transient network and service failures gracefully

faq.question: What is jitter and why is it important?
faq.answer: Jitter adds randomness to retry timing so clients do not all retry at the same instant. Without jitter, thousands of clients retrying at exactly the same exponential intervals create a thundering herd that overwhelms the service again.

faq.question: How many retries should you allow?
faq.answer: Typically three to five retries with exponential backoff is sufficient. Cap the maximum delay to prevent excessively long waits. Combine with a circuit breaker so that after sustained failures, retries stop entirely rather than consuming resources.
